Dr. Todd A. Lefkowitz is a board-certified ophthalmologist who works as an expert ophthalmology witness for attorneys handling eye-care cases in New York. He has already reviewed cases from New York and has testified at trial there, and he takes on work for mainly plaintiff and sometimes defense counsel. He is also licensed to practice medicine in New York.

If you need an expert ophthalmologist witness in New York, most of the work can be done remotely. Records review, calls and depositions happen by phone or video conference, so it does not matter whether your case is in New York City, Buffalo, Albany or a smaller county court.

Ophthalmologist Expert Witness Services in New York

Dr. Lefkowitz can support a New York case from the first look at the records through trial:

  • Review of medical records and a clear opinion on whether the standard of care was met
  • Consulting physician review for a New York certificate of merit
  • Affidavits in support of your case if merited
  • Deposition testimony, in person or by video conference
  • Trial testimony, with travel to New York when needed

Dr. Lefkowitz understands that some cases are time sensitive. Once the case is received, he can offer a quick turnaround.

New York Rules That Shape an Eye Malpractice Case

New York requires a medical malpractice complaint to come with a certificate of merit from the plaintiff's attorney, stating that the attorney reviewed the facts, consulted at least one physician and concluded there is a reasonable basis for the case (CPLR 3012-a). If the filing deadline does not leave time for the consultation, the certificate can be filed within 90 days after the complaint is served.

The filing deadline is two years and six months from the act or omission, or from the last treatment where there is continuous treatment for the same condition (CPLR 214-a). Sending the case for an expert ophthalmology witness review early gives your team time to act on the opinion.

This is general information for attorneys, not legal advice. Your counsel should confirm how these rules apply to your case.

  • Eyelid and oculoplastic surgery
  • LASIK and refractive surgery
  • Glaucoma
  • Retinal detachment
  • Strabismus surgery, pterygium surgery and emergency eye care

Why New York Attorneys Choose Dr. Lefkowitz

  • Board-certified ophthalmologist, Diplomate of the American Board of Ophthalmology since 1982, with over 40 years of practice as a surgeon and clinician

Dr. Lefkowitz is an independent and ethical expert. You can see every state where he has reviewed cases on his expert ophthalmologist witness services page.

How to Start Your New York Case

  1. Email talefkowitzmd@gmail.com or fill in the form on the Contact Me page. Add a short summary of the case, the court and any deadline.
  2. Dr. Lefkowitz replies to talk through the case and confirm it fits his expertise.
  3. Send Dr. Lefkowitz the medical records. He will review them and provide an expert ophthalmology witness report with his opinion.

Please contact Dr. Lefkowitz only if you are an attorney or are working with legal representation.

New York Expert Ophthalmology Witness FAQs

Q

Does Dr. Lefkowitz work for both plaintiff and defense in New York?

Dr. Lefkowitz reviews New York eye cases for mainly plaintiff and sometimes defense counsel, but provides the same independent opinion either way.

Q

Can Dr. Lefkowitz be the physician consulted for a New York certificate of merit?

Yes, if his review supports the case. Under CPLR 3012-a the attorney certifies having consulted at least one physician and concluded there is a reasonable basis for the case. Dr. Lefkowitz can review the records and discuss his opinion before the certificate is signed.

Q

Does he need to travel to New York?

Not for most of the work. Case review and depositions can be done by phone or video conference. He will travel to New York for trial testimony.

Q

How soon should a New York case be sent for review?

As early as possible. New York generally allows two years and six months from the act or omission or the end of continuous treatment (CPLR 214-a). Your counsel should confirm the deadline for your case.
